title: Comparison race: which is faster, live?
summary: Several runs plotted against one clock, a vertical marker at the current time, a leaderboard of progress at that time and a time slider. It teaches you to read a race: what is measured, against what and at which instant.

media.alt: Left panel of three loss curves against time with a vertical marker at 9 seconds and right panel of progress bars for three optimizers, above a time slider.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Which is faster, live?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: wall-clock time in s (0 to 20) against loss on a log axis (0.02 to 1), one line per optimizer; bold up to the marker at t = 9 s, thin afterwards. Right: horizontal bars of progress at t = 9 s: A 91 percent, B 76 percent, C 54 percent. Bottom: the slider.
look_at: Is every run drawn on the same clock and the same scale?
Which curve is lowest at the marker, and by how much?
What does the leaderboard measure, and how is progress defined?
What happens after the marker (the thin lines)? Does the ranking change?
read_the_figure.proves: At the chosen time, one run is further along than another. With a shared clock and axes the comparison is fair. It says nothing about final quality unless the runs are followed to the end.
if_wrong: Runs on different clocks (iterations for one, seconds for another): the race is not fair.
A leaderboard with an undefined measure: what is 91 percent of?
A single race: speed may depend on seed and settings.

terms.meaning: Real elapsed time, as opposed to iterations or epochs.
The quantity being minimised; lower is better.
The fraction of the initial loss removed so far: 1 - L(t)/L(0) (assuming L(0) = 1).
One time value drives every run in the view.
A ranking of runs by a stated measure at the current time.

remember: Same clock, same axes, same starting point.
Progress = 1 - L(t) / L(0), here at t = 9 s.
Time to reach a target loss is the fairer ranking when runs differ in speed over time.
Repeat with other seeds before trusting a race.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position encodes time and loss on a log scale; each run has a colour, a line style and a marker shape so that it survives greyscale; a bold segment marks the history up to now and a thin one the future. The amber vertical line is the clock. Bars on the right encode progress with a hatch per run. The slider at the bottom is the control of time.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A race is a comparison in time, and the eye is good at ranking positions at one instant. The vertical marker converts a family of curves into one number per run, which the bars show, and the slider lets the reader move the instant. A log axis makes constant-rate decay a straight line, so the rate is the slope.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Is the clock shared? Yes: all three curves are drawn on the same axes with the vertical marker at 9 s and the label one clock drives all runs. Q2: What does the leaderboard say? At 9 s A has removed 91 percent of the loss, B 76 percent and C 54 percent, because the losses are 0.087, 0.24 and 0.46 on the curves. Q3: Does the ranking change later? Not within the 20 s shown: the thin curves keep their order, with A falling to about 0.02 at 20 s, B to 0.05 and C to 0.18; but the gap on the log axis is a constant ratio, not a constant difference.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Same clock: it is the whole point of a race. If the runs had separate timers the picture would be a set of animations, not a comparison.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A race at one instant may mislead: a run that leads at 9 s may be overtaken later, and an early lead does not mean a better end result. Progress as 1 - L depends on the loss scale and saturates, so the bars look closer to one another at late times (on a log axis the same ratio looks equal everywhere). Wall-clock time depends on hardware; different seeds and tunings could reverse the ranking. A single run per method has no error bar.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Time to target: bars showing the time each run needs to reach a loss of 0.1. A table with mean and spread over several seeds. A plot of loss against iteration alongside the one against time, because speed per iteration and cost per iteration are different.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a second bar chart with the time to reach L = 0.1 and a band for the spread over 10 seeds on each curve.

steps.title: Loss model and progress at time t
steps.note: With rates r = 0.30, 0.17 and 0.09 per second for A, B and C: 91, 76 and 54 percent at t = 9 s.

steps.title: Time to reach a target loss

worked.title: Progress at 9 s and time to a target
worked.problem: With L(t) = exp(-r t) + 0.02, r = 0.30, 0.17 and 0.09, compute progress at t = 9 s and the time to reach L = 0.1.
worked.answer: 91, 76 and 54 percent at 9 s (as on the leaderboard); A reaches 0.1 at 8.4 s, B at 14.9 s and C at 28.1 s.

analyze.q: The leaderboard at 9 s and the time to target give the same order here. When would they differ?
What does it mean that the lines are straight on the log axis?

evaluate.q: Is one race enough to say optimizer A is better than C?

create: Add a time-to-target bar chart and mark the target on the loss axis.
Run the race with 10 seeds and draw the median with a band.

checks.q: What does the shared clock do?
checks.answer: It makes the runs comparable at each instant.

checks.q: Loss 0.24 at t = 9 s starting from 1. Progress?
Run C is behind A at 9 s. Does that mean C is a worse optimizer?
checks.answer: Not necessarily: one race at one setting shows speed at that time only; test more seeds and compare time to target and final loss.
